note: Adjudicated variants: three orthographic — one a real divergence between the witnesses (Genetríce / Genitríce, both real spellings of the same word), two the house i/j rule against both — and six accidental (punctuation, capitalization). Substantive text otherwise agrees across both witnesses with zero divergence.

adjudicated.ruling: No comma before the et joining the last of the three, with do and with the corpus ruling at ordinarium.aufer-a-nobis w032: prætéritis, præséntibus et futúris is one series governed by malis and the conjunction closes it.

Genetríce, with do and with the 1962 typical edition, which prints Genetrice in this prayer and nowhere Genitrice. Both spellings are the word — genetrix and genitrix are the same noun from gigno, the first the older Latin form — so neither page is wrong; witness do itself sets Genitríce in the Leonine prayers after Mass. The corpus already carries Genetrícis at ordinarium.communicantes w011, and one spelling is kept throughout.

Comma after ut, with do and with the corpus ruling at ordinarium.supplices-te-rogamus w023: the phrase ope misericórdiæ tuæ adiúti is wedged between the conjunction and its verb simus, and the comma marks the interruption.

The j-form against this edition's i-form, by the house rule in ORTHOGRAPHY.md. This edition prints i because the books it edits do: the 1962 typical edition sets Iesu, Ioánnem, iube and maiestátis throughout, and so does the Mszał Rzymski of the Tyniec Benedictines (Pallottinum, Poznań 1963), which is the book a Polish reader is most likely to hold. The mid-century hand missals print j; neither spelling is a different word, and the apparatus records theirs.

No comma before the apposition Fílium tuum, with handmissal-eo and with the corpus ruling at ordinarium.te-igitur w007. The typical edition prints the comma; the corpus keeps its own rule, and the reading is recorded here so the choice is visible.
No comma before Deus, with do. Deus is a predicate standing with vivit et regnat — He lives and reigns as God — not an apposition to be set off; the same ruling governs w073.
Full stop, as at w072. The corpus closes the utterance here because the rubric that follows sends the priest to the words said aloud; handmissal-eo prints no rubrics and so runs the sentence on.
Capital Per, with do and with the corpus reading at ordinarium.per-ipsum w022: the conclusion said aloud is a fresh utterance after the rubric, not the tail of the secret prayer.
